title: Mumbai, Delhi and Jaipur Ranked Among World's Best Street Food Cities
excerpt: Top chefs endorse global rankings as Mumbai's khau gallis and Delhi's Mughlai lanes earn international recognition from Time Out and TasteAtlas.
body:
• Time Out's latest global food rankings place Mumbai, Delhi and Jaipur among the world's best cities for street food, with Mumbai ranking 14th overall among the world's best food destinations.
  • Celebrity chefs Sanjeev Kapoor and Ajay Chopra endorsed the rankings, citing India's unmatched diversity of street food cultures across regions.
  • Mumbai's khau gallis — neighbourhood food streets — received special recognition for their range of chaat, sandwiches, Frankies and falooda.
  • TasteAtlas separately ranked Mumbai 5th globally among the world's best food cities, with five other Indian cities in the top 100.

Three Indian cities have earned prominent positions in the latest international street food rankings, with Mumbai, Delhi and Jaipur recognised as among the best destinations in the world for eating on the go. The rankings, which draw on Time Out's global food surveys, have been endorsed by some of India's most prominent culinary voices.

Celebrity chefs Sanjeev Kapoor and Ajay Chopra both weighed in on the rankings, arguing that the recognition barely scratches the surface of India's street food heritage. India Today surveyed top chefs to assess whether the three cities truly deserve their spots — and the consensus was emphatic.

Mumbai: The Undisputed Capital

Mumbai placed 14th on Time Out's list of the world's 20 best food cities for 2025, the only Indian city to make the cut. The publication singled out the city's famous khau gallis — food streets that run through neighbourhoods from southern Zaveri Bazaar to northern Ghatkopar — as a defining feature.

"The go-to places for a quick fix when hungry are the khau gallis dotting neighbourhoods," Time Out wrote. "Between savoury chaat, jumbo sandwiches, veggie-laden 'pizzas,' Beirut-inspired Frankie wraps, and dry-fruit topped falooda, every bite is far from demure — never subtle and never shy."

The city also secured 5th place on TasteAtlas's separate ranking of the world's 100 best food cities, making it the highest-ranked Indian city on either list. Restaurants such as Ram Ashraya, Shree Thaker Bhojanalay and Cafe Madras were highlighted as must-visit landmarks.

"Mumbai's street food is a melting pot — vada pav from Maharashtrian kitchens, pav bhaji from Gujarati vendors, and South Indian dosas from Udupi joints, all within walking distance of each other."

— Sanjeev Kapoor, Celebrity Chef

Delhi: Where History Meets Hawkers

Delhi's street food scene draws from centuries of Mughal, Punjabi and migrant culinary traditions. The city's chole bhature, nihari, butter chicken, parathas and chaat remain anchors of a food culture that spans the narrow lanes of Old Delhi's Chandni Chowk to the modern food courts of South Delhi.

TasteAtlas ranked Delhi 53rd among the world's best food cities, noting its ability to narrate "stories of emperors, poets and street vendors alike." Chef Ajay Chopra pointed to Delhi's unique position as a city where Mughlai, Punjabi and street food traditions coexist and constantly reinvent each other.

Jaipur: The Emerging Contender

Jaipur's inclusion reflects growing international interest in Rajasthani street food. The Pink City's pyaaz kachori, dal baati churma, ghewar and kulfi have long been regional favourites, but they are now drawing food tourists from abroad. Street food tours in Jaipur have gained traction on global travel platforms, with guides leading visitors through local food stalls that have operated for generations.

Beyond the Rankings

The international recognition extends beyond these three cities. TasteAtlas placed Amritsar at 48th, Hyderabad at 54th, Kolkata at 73rd and Chennai at 93rd in its global top 100. Southern India as a region ranked 40th among the world's 100 best food regions.

The rankings arrive as India's food tourism sector gains momentum. Culinary tours, street food walks and food-focused travel itineraries are increasingly common in marketing by state tourism boards and private operators alike.

The Diaspora Connection

For members of the Indian diaspora, the rankings validate a culinary heritage they carry with them. Street food — from the pani puri of Mumbai to the golgappas of Delhi — often serves as the most visceral connection to home. The international recognition may also spur more diaspora-led food businesses abroad, as Indian street food concepts gain credibility on the global stage.
nri_angle: Street food serves as a visceral connection to home for the diaspora; international validation may spur more Indian street food concepts abroad.
